'''John Norris Bahcall''' (December 30, 1934 – August 17, 2005) was an American [[List of astrophysicists|astrophysicist]] and the Richard Black Professor for Astrophysics at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]]. He was known for a wide range of contributions to solar, galactic and extragalactic astrophysics, including the [[solar neutrino problem]], the development of the [[Hubble Space Telescope]], and his leadership and development of the Institute for Advanced Study in [[Princeton, New Jersey|Princeton]].<ref name="Tremaine">{{cite book |last=Tremaine |first=Scott D. |year=2011 |title=Biographical Memoirs of the National Academy of Sciences |volume= |location= Washington, DC |publisher= The National Academies Press |url=https://www.nasonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/bahcall-john-n.pdf |chapter=John Norris Bahcall 1934-2005 |pages=1–25}}</ref><ref name="Haxton">{{cite journal |last1=Haxton |first1=Wick |date=1 November 2009 |title=The Scientific Life of John Bahcall |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/full/10.1146/annurev.nucl.010909.083722 |journal=Annual Review of Nuclear and Particle Science |language=en |volume=59 |issue=1 |pages=1–20 |arxiv=0904.2865 |bibcode=2009ARNPS..59....1H |doi=10.1146/annurev.nucl.010909.083722 |issn=0163-8998 |s2cid=15314700 |access-date=9 March 2023}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Bahcall was born into a Jewish family in [[Shreveport, Louisiana]] on December 30, 1934,<ref name="Overbye">{{cite news |last1=Overbye |first1=Dennis |title=John N. Bahcall, 70, Dies; Astrophysicist at Princeton |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/08/19/nyregion/john-n-bahcall-70-dies-astrophysicist-at-princeton.html |access-date=9 March 2023 |work=The New York Times |date=19 August 2005}}</ref> and would later describe an early aspiration to become a [[Reform Judaism|Reform]] [[rabbi]].<ref name="Avrahami">{{cite news |last1=Avrahami |first1=Avner |title=Family Affair The Bahcalls |url=https://www.haaretz.com/family-affair-the-bahcalls-1.90945 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150602101337/http://www.haaretz.com/family-affair-the-bahcalls-1.90945 |url-status=dead |archive-date=June 2, 2015 |access-date=9 March 2023 |work=Haaretz |date=June 11, 2003 |language=en}}</ref> He did not take science classes at high school.<ref name="Tremaine"/> In high school he was a state tennis champion<ref name="Haxton"/> and a national debate champion (1952).<ref name="Tremaine"/>

Bahcall began his university studies at [[Louisiana State University]] as a [[philosophy]] student on a tennis scholarship, where he considered pursuing the rabbinate. At the end of his freshman year, he transferred to the [[University of California, Berkeley]], still studying philosophy.<ref name="Tremaine" /> He took his first [[physics]] class to fulfill a graduation science requirement, later saying:<ref name="Wilson" />

{{quote|"It was the hardest thing I have ever done in my life, but I fell in love with science. I was thrilled by the fact that by knowing physics you could figure out how real things worked, like sunsets and airplanes, and that after a while everyone agreed on what was the right answer to a question."<ref name="Wilson"/>}}

Bahcall switched majors to physics,<ref name="Tremaine" /> and graduated with an [[Bachelor of Arts|AB]] in Physics from Berkeley in 1956. He obtained his [[Master of Science|MS]] in physics in 1957 from the [[University of Chicago]] and his [[PhD]] in physics from [[Harvard University]] in 1961.<ref name="Tremaine" /><ref name="Haxton" />

He spent a year as a research fellow in physics with [[Emil Konopinski]] at [[Indiana University Bloomington|Indiana University]]. From 1962 to 1970, he worked with a group led by [[William Alfred Fowler|William Fowler]] at the Kellogg Laboratory of the [[California Institute of Technology]],<ref name="Haxton" /> first as a research fellow and later as an assistant and associate professor.<ref name="AIP" />

==Academic career==
Bahcall joined the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in [[Princeton, New Jersey]] in 1968<ref name="Ostriker">{{cite journal |last1=Ostriker |first1=Jeremiah P. |date=1 September 2005 |title=OBITUARY John Norris Bahcall 1935–2005 Nuclear astrophysicist who uncovered the solar neutrino problem |url=http://www.sns.ias.edu/~jnb/Neta/Natureobituary.pdf |journal=Nature |volume=437 |issue=7055 |page=43 |doi=10.1038/437043a |pmid=16136121 |s2cid=4323443 |access-date=9 March 2023}}</ref><ref name="Tremaine" /> becoming a professor of natural sciences in 1971 and the Richard Black Professor of Natural Sciences in 1997.<ref name="AIP">{{cite web |title=Bahcall, John N. |url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11409023.html |website=The American Institute of Physics |access-date=9 March 2023}}</ref>

Bahcall became a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 1976.<ref>{{Cite web|title=John N. Bahcall|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/john-n-bahcall-qpwbbv/|access-date=2021-10-15|website=www.nasonline.org}}</ref>

He was president of the [[American Astronomical Society]] from 1990 to 1992,<ref name="Wilson">{{cite news |last1=Wilson |first1=Teresa |title=This Month in Astronomical History: Remembering John Bahcall |url=https://aas.org/posts/news/2017/12/month-astronomical-history-remembering-john-bahcall |access-date=9 March 2023 |work=American Astronomical Society |date=12 December 2017}}</ref> and was president-elect of the [[American Physical Society]] at the date of his death.<ref name="APS2005">{{cite journal |title=APS Mourns Loss of President-Elect John Bahcall |journal=APS News |date=October 2005 |volume=14 |issue=9 |url=https://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/200510/bahcall.cfm}}</ref>

==Research==
Bahcall published over six hundred scientific papers<ref name="Ostriker"/> and wrote or edited nine books on astrophysics.<ref name="Haxton"/>

He is most notable for his work in establishing the [[standard solar model]]. He spent much of his life pursuing the [[solar neutrino problem]] with [[physical chemistry|physical chemist]] [[Raymond Davis Jr.|Raymond Davis, Jr]]. Together, Davis and Bahcall collaborated on the [[Homestake Experiment]]. To test Bahcall's theoretical predictions, Davis created an underground [[detector for neutrinos]] in a [[South Dakota]] gold mine, essentially a large tank filled with [[perchloroethylene|cleaning fluid]]. The flux of neutrinos found by the detector was one-third the amount theoretically predicted by Bahcall, a discrepancy that took over thirty years to resolve.<ref name="Haxton"/><ref name="Jelley">{{cite journal |last1=Jelley |first1=Nick |last2=McDonald |first2=Arthur B. |last3=Robertson |first3=R.G. Hamish |title=The Sudbury Neutrino Observatory |journal=Annual Review of Nuclear and Particle Science |date=1 November 2009 |volume=59 |issue=1 |pages=431–465 |doi=10.1146/annurev.nucl.55.090704.151550 |bibcode=2009ARNPS..59..431J |language=en |issn=0163-8998|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Martin">{{cite book |last1=Martin |first1=B. R. |title=Particle physics |date=1997 |publisher=J. Wiley |location=Chichester, England |isbn=978-0-471-97285-3 |edition=2nd |url=https://archive.org/details/particlephysics0000mart_k5d4/page/265 |page=265}}</ref> Bahcall's ongoing research in this area resulted in publication of his book ''Neutrino Astrophysics'' (1989), considered a standard reference on solar neutrinos.<ref name="Tremaine"/><ref>{{cite book |last1=Bahcall |first1=John N. |title=Neutrino astrophysics |date=1989 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge [England] |isbn=978-0-521-37975-5}}</ref>

The 2002 [[Nobel Prize]] in physics was awarded to Davis and [[Masatoshi Koshiba]] for their pioneering work in observing the neutrinos predicted from Bahcall's solar model, thereby vindicating Bahcall's prediction.<ref name="Nobel">{{cite web | url=https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/2002/press.html | title=Press Release: The 2002 Nobel Prize in Physics | publisher=Nobel Media AB | website=nobelprize.org | access-date=2017-03-29}}</ref><ref name="Holley">{{cite news |last1=Holley |first1=Joe |title=Solar Physics Expert John Bahcall Dies |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2005/08/19/AR2005081901735_pf.html |access-date=9 March 2023 |newspaper=Washington Post |date=August 20, 2005}}</ref>

In addition to his work on solar neutrinos, Bahcall collaborated with Eli Waxman on the [[Waxman-Bahcall bound]] for high energy neutrinos. This bound sets a limit on high energy neutrino flux based on the observed flux of high energy [[cosmic rays]]. It was not possible to verify this prediction until after his death, with the construction of neutrino telescopes capable of detecting very high energy neutrinos, such as the [[IceCube Neutrino Observatory]].<ref name="Haxton"/><ref name="Tremaine"/><ref name="Waxman">{{Cite journal |last1=Waxman |first1=Eli |last2=Bahcall |first2=John |year=1999 |title=High energy neutrinos from astrophysical sources: An upper bound |journal=Physical Review D |language=en |volume=59 |issue=2 |article-number=023002 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.59.023002|arxiv=hep-ph/9807282 |bibcode=1998PhRvD..59b3002W |s2cid=38054395 }}</ref>

Another contribution of Bahcall to astrophysics was the development and implementation of the [[Hubble Space Telescope]], in collaboration with [[Lyman Spitzer|Lyman Spitzer, Jr.]], from the 1970s through to the period after the telescope was launched in 1990.<ref name="Haxton"/><ref name="Tremaine"/> 
In 1992, Bahcall received the [[NASA Distinguished Service Medal]] for this work.<ref name="NASA2006"/><ref name="Kaufman">{{cite news |last1=Kaufman |first1=Ron |title=People: John Bahcall Receives Award From NASA For His Work On Hubble Space Telescope |url=https://www.the-scientist.com/profession/people-john-bahcall-receives-award-from-nasa-for-his-work-on-hubble-space-telescope-60096 |access-date=9 March 2023 |work=The Scientist Magazine® |date=May 24, 1992 |language=en}}</ref> He reintroduced the traditional method of star counts, as a quantitative tool for assessing galactic structure.<ref name="Pinsonneault">{{cite journal|last=Pinsonneault|first=M.|title=The Legacy of John Bahcall|journal=[[ASP Conference Series]]|date=2008 |url=https://adsabs.harvard.edu/full/2008ASPC..384....3P |volume=384|page=3|bibcode=2008ASPC..384....3P}}</ref>

The standard model of a galaxy, with a massive [[black hole]] surrounded by stars, is known as the [[Bahcall-Wolf model]]. The Bahcall-Soneira model was for many years the standard model for the structure of the [[Milky Way]]. He also contributed to accurate astrophysical models of stellar interiors.<ref name="Haxton"/><ref name="Tremaine"/>

== Personal life and death ==
Bahcall married [[Princeton University]] astrophysics professor [[Neta Bahcall]], whom he met as a graduate student at the [[Weizmann Institute]] in the 1960s. They had a daughter and two sons (including [[Safi Bahcall]]).<ref name="Haxton" /><ref name="Ostriker" />

He died in New York on 17 August 2005, from a rare blood disorder.<ref name="Holley" /><ref name="Overbye" />
